newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Duisenberg sees some EU members missing EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Duisenberg sees some EU members missing EMU start.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg said on Monday a number of European Union (EU) members will not be able to take part in European economic and monetary union (EMU) when it begins on January 1, 1999.
He said many EU member states were making desperate attempts to meet the convergence criteria for the introduction of the euro single currency in Europe.
"Nevertheless we must make allowance for the fact that a number of them will not be able to participate when EMU takes off on January 1, 1999," Duisenberg said in a speech in Frankfurt.

"We should not make too much of their predicament. After all, a member state with a derogation is not excommunicated but will be allowed to join at a later date," he said on receiving the European Banker of the Year award in Frankfurt.

Derogation is the term for a state which is accepted to be unable or unwilling to carry out provisions for an obligatory EU matter. A copy of the speech was made available by the Dutch central bank, the Nederlandsche Bank, in Amsterdam.
Duisenberg will take over on July 1 as the head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of the European Central Bank (ECB), which will be set once a single currency is introduced.
He said that if these countries met the critera within the near future, some would be able to join the core group of EMU members when euro banknotes and coins were introduced in 2002.

He also said discussion on EMU was increasingly centering on the question of how, rather than whether, to achieve monetary union. This was only right because the completion of EMU became a certainty when it was laid down in the Maastricht Treaty in 1992.

By signing and ratifying the treaty, member states opted to join EMU as soon as they fulfilled the criteria, with only Britain and Denmark insisting on an opt-out clause releasing them from the obligation to join when they qualified.
"The completion of EMU is irreversible, the introduction of the euro definitive," Duisenberg said.

He said it was of the utmost importance for EMU to make a proper start, with the euro being just as hard as the Dutch guilder or the German mark. "If we want the euro to be strong, there is nothing for it but to comply strictly with with the convergence criteria," Duisenberg said.
He also said an exchange rate mechanism was being designed to ensure that "derogation" countries retained close links with the core group.

It aimed to prevent large currency fluctuations within the EU but efforts would have to be made to reinforce convergence between so-called "ins and outs" to ensure the derogation countries eventually joined EMU.
Duisenberg said the pact for stability and growth, under which members must seek budgets near-balance or in surplus, would make a major contribution.
